title: Compassion Benchmark Daily Briefing -- July 26, 2026
headline: Tunis gets its first real assessment, and the published score turns out to be 11.9 points too high.
summary: Twenty governments, cities, and companies were reviewed overnight. Seventeen scores held within the benchmark's five-point confirmation range. Tunis had never been individually assessed. A first real review, done as thousands marched in the capital demanding the president's resignation, found conditions 11.9 points worse than the placeholder score implied. Uganda's evidence, a military siege of the country's largest independent newsroom, would cross the country from Developing into Critical, but the strongest available source is one tier below the benchmark's bar for moving a score across a band line, so the finding is logged and the published score of 20.3 stands. Kathmandu, assessed for the first time, landed exactly on the line the benchmark uses to decide whether a finding becomes a formal proposal. For a third consecutive night, the benchmark's own news scan cited an old event as if it were new, and a second check caught it before any score moved. None of tonight's three proposals has been applied. All three published scores are unchanged: Tunis at 34.4, Uganda at 20.3, and Kathmandu at 18.8.

pipeline.queueHandling: Tunis's first-ever assessment produced a straightforward downgrade finding, logged as pending. Uganda's band-crossing evidence and Kathmandu's first-baseline reading were both held to the benchmark's sourcing standard rather than asserted outright. All three published scores are unchanged: Tunis at 34.4, Uganda at 20.3, Kathmandu at 18.8.

topSignals.title: Tunis Was Never Actually Assessed Until Tonight, and the First Real Review Finds It Nearly 12 Points Worse
topSignals.whyItMatters: Tunis's published score sat unchanged for years because no one had individually assessed the city. A first real review, done as thousands marched for the president's resignation, finds conditions far worse than the placeholder implied.
topSignals.description: Tunis's published score of 34.4 out of 100 was a bulk-import placeholder, numerically identical to the pre-assessment seed value Tunisia the country carried before its own first review. Tunis itself had never been individually assessed. A first evidence-based review this cycle finds a much lower 22.5, a movement of 11.9 points, still within the Developing band. Human Rights Watch reported on July 8, 2026 that five years after President Kais Saied seized extraordinary executive powers, repression of civil society, journalists, lawyers, and migrants has become systematic, and that UN independent experts have condemned the prosecution and sentencing of judges and human rights defenders. On July 25, 2026, thousands marched down Habib Bourguiba Avenue in central Tunis demanding Saied's resignation. The finding has been logged as a downgrade recommendation. It has not been applied, and the published score of 34.4 is unchanged.

evidence.quote: Five years after Tunisian President Kais Saied seized extraordinary executive powers, the country's human rights situation has deteriorated dramatically.
We are not tenants of this country, we are its owners.
evidence.claim: Thousands rallied in central Tunis on July 25, 2026, demanding the president resign.
The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights called on Tunisia to end repressive measures against civil society and media.

topSignals.title: Uganda's Military-Siege Evidence Would Cross a Score Boundary, and the Benchmark Held It to a Higher Sourcing Standard
topSignals.whyItMatters: The army seized government critics and besieged the country's largest independent newsroom. The evidence is real, but the benchmark's rule for moving a score across a boundary line has not yet been met.
topSignals.description: Uganda's published score of 20.3 out of 100 sits at the bottom edge of the Developing band. Human Rights Watch reported on July 16, 2026 that since mid-June, security forces have unlawfully seized at least five critics of President Yoweri Museveni and his son, UPDF chief General Muhoozi Kainerugaba, and that since June 28 the military has surrounded and laid siege to Nation Media Group, Uganda's largest independent media company, after Kainerugaba ordered its television and newspaper operations shut down. Based on that evidence, researchers calculated a lower score of 13.1, which would cross Uganda from Developing into the Critical band. But before a score can cross a band line, the benchmark requires at least two independent sources, with at least one from top-tier journalism, a court record, or a government filing. The strongest source found is Human Rights Watch, one tier below that bar. A UN Secretary-General note on the same pattern exists but is dated July 2, before the evidence window opened. The finding has been logged, not applied, and Uganda's published score remains 20.3.

evidence.quote: Since mid-June 2026, security forces have unlawfully seized at least five critics of President Yoweri Museveni and his son, General Muhoozi Kainerugaba, the chief of the Uganda People's Defence Force (UPDF).

Since June 28, the military has surrounded and laid siege to the premises of the Nation Media Group, Uganda's largest independent media company, after Kainerugaba ordered the shutdown of its television and newspaper operations.
President Museveni's government is increasingly using the military as a cudgel against dissent and criticism
evidence.source: Carine Kaneza Nantulya, Human Rights Watch

evidence.claim: A rights group condemned the abduction of government critics by the Ugandan military.

topSignals.title: Kathmandu Gets Its First Real Assessment, and the Finding Lands Exactly on the Benchmark's Threshold
topSignals.whyItMatters: Kathmandu had never been individually assessed. The first real review lands exactly on the five-point line the benchmark uses to decide whether a movement becomes a formal proposal.
topSignals.description: Kathmandu's published score of 18.8 out of 100 was a placeholder with no evidence behind any dimension value; the city had never been individually assessed. Police detained three activists on July 11, 2026 after they visited a Kirtipur holding centre sheltering families displaced by forced evictions and flooding. One of them, Majid Ansari, was discharged from hospital on July 15 after five days, still in custody, and told reporters he had received no arrest papers while officers pressured him to sign a document. Police disputed his account, saying he was not arrested and was injured when two sides clashed at the holding centre gate. Amnesty International Nepal called for his immediate and unconditional release. A first evidence-based review finds a score of 13.8, a movement of exactly 5.0 points, the benchmark's own threshold for a formal proposal, and does not cross a band (both scores are Critical). Because a five-point move on a first-ever assessment is partly a change in what has been measured rather than a change in conduct, and because the evidence rests largely on one newspaper group plus one advocacy statement, the finding has been logged for review rather than applied. The published score of 18.8 is unchanged.

evidence.quote: I have not received any arrest papers. Police officers keep coming and pressuring me to sign a document, but I have refused.
He was not arrested. Police intervened when two sides clashed at the holding centre gate, and he was injured in the process.
evidence.claim: Police denied the arrest and attributed the injury to a clash.
evidence.source: Nepal Police, quoted by The Kathmandu Post

evidence.claim: Amnesty International called for the immediate and unconditional release of the detained activist and for the right to protest to be ensured.

topSignals.title: For a Third Consecutive Night, the Benchmark Caught a News Event Mis-Dated Against an Old Article, and Fixed It
topSignals.whyItMatters: A Pentagon designation from June was almost scored as if it happened in July, for the third night running. A tightened check still cannot catch this class of error from a web address alone, so a second read confirmed the real dates before anything reached a published score.
topSignals.description: Six items were corrected or dropped tonight on date-verification grounds, the third consecutive night this class of error has appeared. Unitree Robotics: the scan placed a Pentagon designation of the company as Chinese military-linked technology on July 20, 2026, the date of a news article about it. The actual Department of Defense designation was made on June 8, 2026, corroborated by a technology-press report and a law-firm client alert from that same week; it was moved to background, outside the evidence window. A second claim, that Unitree's G1 humanoid continuously transmits sensor data to Chinese servers, had no dated source anywhere and was dropped entirely rather than treated as likely true. Kuala Lumpur: a migrant-labor advocacy letter was addressed to Bangladesh's head of government ahead of a state visit to Malaysia; the scan had reversed the addressee and recorded it as a demand made of the Malaysian government. Tunis: a rally reported by Al Jazeera on July 26 actually took place the day before, Saturday July 25; the event was re-dated, and both dates remain inside the evidence window. Boston Dynamics: the prior assessment recorded Hyundai's acquisition as completing on July 16, which was actually a June stake purchase; multiple sources place the real closing date at July 20, 2026. Agilent Technologies: reported staff cuts at its Biovectra subsidiary, and a claim of repeated one-to-three percent annual workforce reductions, could not be tied to any dated statement and were not scored. A gate tightened on July 27 blocks undated sourcing, but it checks a source's own publish date, not every date claimed inside a summary; that gap is what let the Unitree article-date error through for a third time. Each of the six was caught and corrected before it reached a published score.

evidence.claim: The Department of Defense added Unitree (Hangzhou Yushu Technology) to its Section 1260H list of Chinese military-linked companies on June 8, 2026, not July 20 as a later article implied.
A migrant-welfare advocacy letter was addressed to Bangladesh's prime minister ahead of a state visit to Malaysia, not to the Malaysian government as the scan first recorded.

topSignals.title: Seven Findings Tonight Turned on Where the Harm Happened, Not Just Whether It Happened
topSignals.whyItMatters: Floods in southeastern Bangladesh, abductions attributed to Tigray authorities, and violence near Johannesburg clinics were all real. None of them lowered the government or city blamed for them, because the benchmark scores an entity for its own conduct, not for harm that happened nearby or was done by someone else.
topSignals.description: The benchmark's attribution rule was applied to seven entities tonight. Dhaka: flash floods killed at least 44 people in southeastern Bangladesh, several hundred kilometers from the capital, and are not scored against the city; police baton-charging students who were protesting exams held during the floods is Dhaka's own conduct, and is scored. Addis Ababa: thousands rallied at Meskel Square on July 18, 2026 against abductions and forced recruitment attributed to authorities in the Tigray region, hundreds of kilometers north; that harm is not scored against the city, though permitting the rally is noted as a mild, not a general, positive. Johannesburg: assaults on foreign nationals by the vigilante group Operation Dudula are non-state conduct and are not scored against the city; the failure to keep public clinics accessible while Nigeria evacuated 1,490 of its citizens is municipal conduct, and is scored. Niger: attacks by jihadist armed groups are not scored against the state; extending pretrial detention to four years the week a rights defender's lawyers sought his release is the state's own conduct, and is scored. Eswatini, a split decision: the United States' transfer of detainees to Eswatini is US conduct; the men's continued detention without charge and denial of confidential legal access inside Eswatini are the country's own conduct. Kuala Lumpur: national labor-recruitment policy is a Malaysian federal matter, not Kuala Lumpur City Hall conduct, and informs the city's score only as sector context. Boston Dynamics: the Ulsan labor dispute is between Hyundai Motor's union and Hyundai Motor; it is scored against Boston Dynamics only where the company's own product and deployment design is implicated.

evidence.claim: Flash floods and landslides killed at least 44 people in southeastern Bangladesh, several hundred kilometers from Dhaka; police baton-charged students in the capital who were protesting exams held during the floods.
An anti-migrant group blocked foreign nationals from public clinics west of Johannesburg while Nigeria evacuated 1,490 of its citizens between June 10 and July 15, 2026.

topSignals.title: Four Apparent Improvements Tonight Were Screened Out as Noise, Not Real Findings
topSignals.whyItMatters: Vanuatu, Florida, Hong Kong, and Addis Ababa each looked like they might be improving this cycle. None of the increases held up as genuine new conduct once checked a second time.
topSignals.description: Anti-false-positive screening set aside four apparent upward movements tonight. Vanuatu: commentary published July 24, 2026 found that Vanuatu's International Court of Justice climate victory has not yet produced repaired water systems, restored electricity, or coastal protection, but that gap was already priced into the score when the published composite was raised on May 23, 2026 following the General Assembly follow-up resolution; re-scoring it again would double count the same event, so no new movement was recorded in either direction. Florida: a review of the state's execution record is real and scored for the first time, but the underlying facts, ten executions by mid-July and the state's death-row exoneration record, were already available at Florida's first evidence-based baseline on July 19, 2026; treating it as a fresh downgrade now would be reviewer-to-reviewer variance rather than new conduct, so it was held sub-threshold with a watch flag instead of a formal proposal. Hong Kong: the government opened 29 shelters and published same-day situation reports as Typhoon Noul made landfall on July 26, 2026, but a competent response to one moderate storm is not evidence of a structural change in how the city treats people, so the score was left effectively unchanged. Addis Ababa: permitting one demonstration that aligned with the federal government's own position is not evidence of a general tolerance for dissent, and was not used to raise the score.

evidence.claim: Vanuatu's International Court of Justice climate victory has not yet produced repaired water systems, restored electricity, or coastal protection for communities facing recurring floods and landslides.
Florida carried out ten executions by mid-July 2026, the most of any state, while also leading the country in death-row exonerations.

topSignals.title: Two Index-Maintenance Issues Surfaced Tonight, Neither a Conduct Finding
topSignals.whyItMatters: A scoring-math gap on Vanuatu and a one-rank positioning drift across 324 other entries are both flagged for cleanup, not because any entity's conduct changed.
topSignals.description: Two data-quality items were referred for index maintenance rather than filed as conduct findings. Vanuatu's published composite of 41.4 does not reconstruct from its own stored dimension values, which yield 42.8 under the benchmark's canonical formula, a difference of 1.4 points, outside the standard 0.5-point tolerance; the benchmark's own automated index check independently flags this gap and separately notes that Vanuatu carries a manual composite override that is not on the approved override list. Separately, 324 entities elsewhere in the published indexes carry a one-position ranking drift against a from-scratch recount; in every one of those cases the composite score and the letter-grade band match exactly, so no entity's score or classification is wrong, only its numeric list position. Neither issue reflects a change in any entity's conduct, and neither was scored as a finding.

Whether Nation Media Group resumes operations, and whether the seized critics are produced in court, are the clearest forward signals.

A court record on the detention's legal basis, or a Nepal Police statement beyond the quoted denial, would raise the confidence of a first-baseline reading that currently sits exactly at the benchmark's proposal threshold.

emergingRisks.detail: The benchmark's own automated index check flags both the reconstruction gap and an unlisted manual override on Vanuatu's composite. Neither reflects a change in conduct; both are referred for maintenance.

sectorAlerts.sector: Countries -- A First Baseline, a Held Band Crossing, and Four Confirmations Under the Attribution Rule
sectorAlerts.headline: Uganda's band-crossing evidence was held to the sourcing bar; Eswatini and Niger confirmed on real detention findings; Vanuatu's apparent gain was screened out as already priced in.
observations: Uganda (20.3 published, 13.1 proposed): a military siege of the country's largest independent newsroom would cross Developing into Critical, but the strongest source sits one tier below the benchmark's band-crossing bar.
Eswatini (9.4) and Niger (12.5): both confirmed after documented detention findings, a US-Eswatini transfer arrangement and a Niger pretrial-detention extension respectively.

Vanuatu (41.4): an apparent +1.7 reading was screened to near-zero once a May 2026 applied change already priced the same evidence; a separate math-hygiene gap was referred for index maintenance, not scored.

sectorAlerts.sector: Global Cities -- Two First-Ever Assessments and Four Confirmations Under the Attribution Rule
sectorAlerts.headline: Tunis and Kathmandu were assessed for the first time; Dhaka, Addis Ababa, Johannesburg, and Kuala Lumpur confirmed with the attribution rule doing most of the work.
observations: Tunis (34.4 published, 22.5 proposed): the city's published score was an un-assessed placeholder; a first real review found systematic repression documented across five years of rule by decree.
Kathmandu (18.8 published, 13.8 proposed): a first-ever review landed exactly on the benchmark's five-point proposal threshold.
Dhaka (23.4), Addis Ababa (18.8), and Johannesburg (32.8): all confirmed under the attribution rule, which scores a city's own conduct rather than harm inflicted nearby or by another actor.
Kuala Lumpur (40.6): the scan had reversed the addressee of a migrant-labor advocacy letter, attributing to Malaysia a demand actually made of Bangladesh.

sectorAlerts.sector: Robotics Labs -- A Third-Night Date Correction and a Buyout-Day Strike
sectorAlerts.headline: Unitree's Pentagon designation was mis-dated for a third consecutive night; Boston Dynamics confirmed after Hyundai's buyout closed the same day 35,000 workers struck over Atlas.
observations: Unitree Robotics (35.9): a Pentagon designation was corrected from a July article date to its true June 8, 2026 date; an undated claim about sensor-data transmission was dropped entirely.
Boston Dynamics (65.6): Hyundai's full acquisition closed July 20, 2026, the same day Ulsan workers escalated a strike demanding written guarantees before Atlas enters a Korean production floor.

sectorAlerts.sector: Fortune 500 -- Five Rotation Checks Where No News Was the Finding
sectorAlerts.headline: Apple's DOJ settlement talks and Citigroup's arbitrated wage claims were the standout findings; A.O. Smith, ADP, Aon, and Agilent confirmed largely on standing structure.
observations: Apple (59.4): in early settlement talks with the Department of Justice over the 2024 iPhone antitrust case, sitting 0.6 points below the Established boundary.
Citigroup (62.5): a federal judge sent former employees' wage-underpayment claims to arbitration on July 24, 2026, closing the question to public view.
A.O. Smith, ADP, Aon, and Agilent Technologies (60.9-77.9): all confirmed on rotation; Aon's standing 14-month data-breach detection gap was the most substantive finding among the four.

methodologyNotes.name: A Third Consecutive Night of Catching the Benchmark's Own Scanner Citing Old News as Current
methodologyNotes.description: For a third night running, the benchmark's nightly news scan cited an event that had already happened, mis-dated as new: a Pentagon designation of Unitree Robotics from June was nearly scored as a July event, the same failure pattern caught on July 24 and July 25. A gate tightened on July 27 blocks sourcing with no date at all, but it checks a source's own publish date, not every date claimed inside a summary against the date embedded in the article itself. A second read caught the error before it reached a published score, which is what the internal check is designed to do.

methodologyNotes.name: A Band Crossing Needs Two Sources, One of Them Strong, Before a Score Moves
methodologyNotes.description: Before any score can cross from one band into another, for example from Developing into Critical, the benchmark requires at least two independent sources, with at least one from top-tier journalism, a court record, or a government filing. Uganda's evidence this cycle, a real military siege of the country's largest independent newsroom, would support a band crossing, but the strongest available source is one tier below that bar. The finding is logged as a lower-confidence reading rather than applied to the published score. Treat the published score as the standing record and the documented evidence pattern as the higher-confidence signal to watch.

methodologyNotes.name: A First-Ever Assessment Is Read as a New Baseline, Not as a Score Decline
methodologyNotes.description: Tunis and Kathmandu had never been individually assessed; their published scores were placeholders. When a first evidence-based review finds a lower number, that is a change in what has been measured, not necessarily a change in conduct. Kathmandu's move landed exactly at the benchmark's five-point threshold for a formal proposal, which is why it was logged for review rather than treated as a straightforward downgrade.

methodologyNotes.name: Conduct Is Scored, Not Proximity to Harm
methodologyNotes.description: The benchmark scores what a government or city does, not what happens near it or to it. Tonight this rule applied to seven entities: Dhaka, Addis Ababa, Johannesburg, Niger, Eswatini, Kuala Lumpur, and Boston Dynamics each held or moved only on their own conduct, while harm inflicted by floods, a foreign militia, a vigilante group, national policy, or a parent company's labor dispute was set aside.

dailyOpeningQuestion.text: Uganda's proposed downgrade would cross the Developing-to-Critical boundary, but its strongest source, Human Rights Watch, sits at source tier 3, one level below the benchmark's band-crossing bar. Would a dated, in-window UN statement on the same pattern satisfy the required tier-4 threshold?
